questions.knowledge_point: Applying Variation of Parameters to a Second-Order Inhomogeneous ODE
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+2y={x}^{3}{e}^{5x}.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ and ${y}_{2}={e}^{2x}.$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${u}_{2}(x)=\int g(x)\,\text{d}x,$ find the function $g.$
questions.worked_solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x)={x}^{3}{e}^{5x}.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{2x}.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{x})({e}^{2x})^{′}-({e}^{x})^{′}({e}^{2x}) \\  & =({e}^{x})(2{e}^{2x})-({e}^{x})({e}^{2x}) \\  & =2{e}^{3x}-{e}^{3x} \\  & ={e}^{3x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}({e}^{2x})^{′}={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for ${u}_{2}.$ We start by eliminating ${u}_{1}^{′}$ from the second equation:

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}=-\frac{{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{x}}=-{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{x}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ (-{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{x}){e}^{x}+2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ -{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{2}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{3}{e}^{5x}}{{e}^{2x}} \\ {u}_{2}^{′} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{2}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{3}{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{2} & =\int {x}^{3}{e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x)={x}^{3}{e}^{3x}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}={e}^{2x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{2x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{2x})^{′}.
$$

We can form a constraint that relates ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}$ by differentiating ${y}_{p}$ and equating this expression to our constraint on ${y}_{p}^{′}.$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{2x})}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}{e}^{x})}^{′}+{({u}_{2}{e}^{2x})}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}({e}^{2x})^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{2}{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{2}{e}^{2x} & ={u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{2x})^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{2}{e}^{2x} & ={u}_{1}{e}^{x}+2{u}_{2}{e}^{2x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+\cancel{{u}_{1}{e}^{x}}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}+\cancel{2{u}_{2}{e}^{2x}} & =\cancel{{u}_{1}{e}^{x}}+\cancel{2{u}_{2}{e}^{2x}}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}=0.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+2y={x}^{3}{e}^{5x}.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ and ${y}_{2}={e}^{2x}.$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${u}_{1}(x)=-\int g(x)\,\text{d}x,$ find the function $g.$
questions.worked_solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x)={x}^{3}{e}^{5x}.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{2x}.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{x})({e}^{2x})^{′}-({e}^{x})^{′}({e}^{2x}) \\  & =({e}^{x})(2{e}^{2x})-({e}^{x})({e}^{2x}) \\  & =2{e}^{3x}-{e}^{3x} \\  & ={e}^{3x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{({e}^{x})}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{({e}^{2x})}^{′}={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for ${u}_{1}.$ We start by eliminating ${u}_{2}^{′}$ from the second equation:

$$
{u}_{2}^{′}=-\frac{{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}}=-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{2x} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+2(-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}){e}^{2x} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}-2{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ -{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{5x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′} & =-{x}^{3}{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{1}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int -{x}^{3}{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{1} & =-\int {x}^{3}{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x)={x}^{3}{e}^{4x}.$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

According to the method of variation of parameters, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={{field-1}}
$$

where ${u}_{1}={u}_{1}(x),{u}_{2}={u}_{2}(x),$ that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-2}}.
$$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x,$ we obtain

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore, we have the following constraint equation relating ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}:$

$$
{{field-4}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x),\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x).
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x).
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x))^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x))^{′}.
$$

We can form a constraint that relates ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}$ by differentiating ${y}_{p}$ and equating this expression to our constraint on ${y}_{p}^{′}.$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x))}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x))}^{′}+{({u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x))}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+{u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x))^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x))^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+5{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-5{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+5{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-5{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x) & ={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x))^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x))^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+5{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-5{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x) & =5{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-5{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+\cancel{5{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\cancel{5{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)} & =\cancel{5{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)}-\cancel{5{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)=0.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}+2y={x}^{2}.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-x}$ and ${y}_{2}={e}^{-2x}.$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${u}_{2}(x)=-\int g(x)\,\text{d}x,$ find the function $g.$
questions.worked_solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x)={x}^{2}.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-2x}.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{-x})({e}^{-2x})^{′}-({e}^{-x})^{′}({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =({e}^{-x})(-2{e}^{-2x})-(-{e}^{-x})({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =-2{e}^{-3x}+{e}^{-3x} \\  & =-{e}^{-3x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{({e}^{-x})}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{({e}^{-2x})}^{′}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}-\,{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for ${u}_{2}.$ We start by eliminating ${u}_{1}^{′}$ from the second equation:

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}=-\frac{{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}}{{e}^{-x}}=-{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\,{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & ={x}^{2} \\ -\,(-{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-x}){e}^{-x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & ={x}^{2} \\ -\,{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{2}^{′} & =-{x}^{2}{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{2}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int -{x}^{2}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{2} & =-\int {x}^{2}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x)={x}^{2}{e}^{2x}.$
